# Security and Compliance

Dimension covering security implications of routing LLM traffic through
third-party gateways. See [citations.md](../citations.md) for source details.

## Data Handling by Provider

| Gateway | Default Logging | Training Opt-out | ZDR Available | EU Routing |
|---------|----------------|------------------|---------------|------------|
| OpenRouter | Provider-dependent [4] | Yes (account setting) [4] | Yes [53] | Yes (eu.openrouter.ai) [4] |
| Portkey | 40+ data points/req [76] | N/A (gateway, not training) | Via enterprise | Yes (geo-routing) [52] |
| LiteLLM Cloud | Usage data only, no message content [13] | N/A | Self-host for full control | Infra on GCP/AWS [13] |
| LiteLLM Self-hosted | No data to LiteLLM servers [13] | N/A | Inherent | User controls |

**OpenRouter data policies [4]:**
- Does not implement uniform logging — routes to providers with their own
  data practices
- Users can opt out of training in account settings; OpenRouter will not route
  to providers that train on data
- Setting has "no bearing on OpenRouter's own policies and what we do with
  your prompts" [4]
- EU endpoint (eu.openrouter.ai) keeps data within European Union [4]

**ZDR significance [20]:** "Stored data is discoverable data, regardless of
what the privacy policy promises." A Dec 2025 court case ordered OpenAI to
produce 20 million ChatGPT logs [20]. ZDR means no storage beyond brief
in-memory processing [53].

## API Key Management

**BYOK (Bring Your Own Key) support:**
- OpenRouter: BYOK with 5% usage fee [2]
- Portkey: Virtual keys with vault storage, rotation, revocation [10]
- LiteLLM: API keys encrypted at rest in PostgreSQL, virtual keys for
  access control [13]
- Cloudflare AI Gateway: Keys stored with alias identification [10]

**LiteLLM key security [13]:** Only sensitive data encrypted at rest (LLM
API keys, provider credentials, config secrets, virtual keys) using
LITELLM_MASTER_KEY. TLS 1.2/1.3 for transit encryption.

**Best practice:** AWS IAM role-based access eliminates need to transmit
credentials for AWS Bedrock [13].

**LiteLLM certifications detail [13]:** SOC 2 Type I and Type II certified.
ISO 27001 certified. Reports available on Enterprise plan. Comprehensive ISMS
(Information Security Management System). Zero high/critical vulnerabilities
in current builds (Grype scanning). CodeQL for code analysis.

## Supply Chain Risk: LiteLLM Incident

**Timeline [16]:**
- March 24, 2026, 10:39 UTC: Malicious versions published to PyPI
- ~16:00 UTC (same day): PyPI quarantined packages after ~40 minutes exposure
- March 30: Clean version v1.83.0 released via new CI/CD v2 pipeline

**Impact [16][50]:** Versions 1.82.7/1.82.8 contained credential stealer
targeting environment variables, SSH keys, cloud provider credentials (AWS,
GCP, Azure), Kubernetes tokens, database passwords. Data encrypted and
exfiltrated to models.litellm.cloud (non-official domain).

**Not affected [16]:** Official Docker image users (pinned dependencies),
LiteLLM Cloud users, users on v1.82.6 or earlier.

**Resolution [16]:** Compromised packages removed, maintainer credentials
rotated, Google Mandiant engaged for forensic analysis, new CI/CD v2 pipeline
with isolated environments.

**Implication:** Self-hosted gateways eliminate third-party data interception
but introduce supply chain risk. Pinned dependencies and verified Docker
images are essential.

## Audit Trails

**Portkey [76]:** Enterprise audit logging, governance layer tracks who
accessed what data and why. 40+ data points per request. Rich logging with
RBAC, workspace/role/budget/rate limit tracking.

**OpenRouter [76]:** Operational billing data and provider-level performance
metrics. Does NOT provide request-level tracing or integration with external
monitoring tools.

**LiteLLM [13]:** Logs spend per virtual key, user, and project. Admin
dashboard UI. Enterprise features include SSO/SAML and audit logs.

## Prompt Injection Risk

OWASP lists prompt injection as the #1 risk for LLM applications [49].
31 out of 36 tested LLM-integrated applications were susceptible [49].
No 100% foolproof solution to indirect prompt injection exists [49].

**Gateway-specific risks:**
- Gateway itself represents a trust boundary — must trust the operator not to
  log, inspect, or manipulate prompts/responses
- Self-hosted solutions eliminate third-party interception risk
- Data provenance and validation can verify external data sources [49]

## Self-Hosted Security Trade-offs

**Advantages [13]:**
- No data transmitted to external servers
- All processing remains on-premises
- Full control over encryption, key management, access controls
- Can use IAM roles for cloud models (eliminating credential transmission)
- Compliance easier when data never leaves your network

**Disadvantages:**
- Self-management of security updates and patches
- Responsibility for securing infrastructure
- Must implement own monitoring, logging, audit trails
- Supply chain risks in dependencies (LiteLLM March 2026 incident [16])

## Gaps and Limitations

- OpenRouter's compliance certifications are not publicly disclosed [7]
- No provider publishes details on prompt/response interception controls
- Data retention specifics for operational purposes (billing, monitoring)
  under ZDR are unclear
- Provider pass-through logging (does OpenAI still log when using BYOK through
  a gateway?) is not documented
- Encryption key management (customer-managed vs provider-managed) is not
  detailed by most gateways
- Geographic routing verification mechanisms (how to prove data stays in-region)
  are not described
